title: Bertrand Russell Explains Why Karl Marx’s Philosophy Produced the Disaster of Communism

body:
in History, Philosophy, Politics |   	September 7th, 2026  3 Comments
	
			

	

In 1927, Bertrand Rus­sell deliv­ered a lec­ture titled “Why I Am Not a Chris­t­ian.” At the time, such a dec­la­ra­tion was still fair­ly bold, as was the rea­son­ing he pro­vid­ed for it. Near­ly three decades there­after, he includ­ed in his col­lec­tion Por­traits from Mem­o­ry anoth­er, short­er piece, “Why I Am Not a Com­mu­nist.” That descrip­tion was safe to apply to one­self in 1954, at least in the main­stream of the Eng­lish-speak­ing world. It would have been riski­er for those who moved in intel­lec­tu­al cir­cles, as a cel­e­brat­ed philoso­pher like Rus­sell most cer­tain­ly did. What’s more, his crit­i­cism extend­ed not just to com­mu­nism as then instan­ti­at­ed by cer­tain soci­eties in the world, but to the thought of Karl Marx him­self.
Rus­sell makes two charges against Marx: “one, that he was mud­dle-head­ed; and the oth­er, that his think­ing was almost entire­ly inspired by hatred.” In his view, the author of Cap­i­tal com­mits intel­lec­tu­al fraud by oppor­tunis­ti­cal­ly accept­ing Thomas Malthus’ dire pre­dic­tion of pop­u­la­tion growth (while reject­ing it at oth­er times), as well as apply­ing David Ricar­do’s the­o­ry of val­ue, which describes it as a kind of embod­ied labor, to wages but not the prices of man­u­fac­tured goods.
“He is entire­ly sat­is­fied with the result, not because it is in accor­dance with the facts or because it is log­i­cal­ly coher­ent, but because it is cal­cu­lat­ed to rouse fury in wage-earn­ers.” Marx sees their upris­ing against cap­i­tal­ists as inevitable due to his “exten­sion to world his­to­ry of cer­tain fea­tures promi­nent in Eng­land and France a hun­dred years ago” and belief in “a cos­mic force called Dialec­ti­cal Mate­ri­al­ism which gov­erns human his­to­ry inde­pen­dent­ly of human voli­tions.”
This dis­missal of Marx’s world­view as “mere mythol­o­gy” has some­thing in com­mon with Rus­sel­l’s cri­tique of Chris­tian­i­ty, and not coin­ci­den­tal­ly so. “I think one of the trou­bles of the world has been the habit of dog­mat­i­cal­ly believ­ing some­thing or oth­er,” he says in the clip above. “I think we ought always to enter­tain our opin­ions with some mea­sure of doubt.” And “if a phi­los­o­phy is to bring hap­pi­ness, it should be inspired by kind­ly feel­ing. Now, Marx is not inspired by kind­ly feel­ing. Marx pre­tend­ed that he want­ed the hap­pi­ness of the pro­le­tari­at, but he real­ly want­ed is the unhap­pi­ness of the bour­geois. And it was because of that neg­a­tive ele­ment, because of that hate ele­ment that his phi­los­o­phy pro­duced dis­as­ter.” There are, per­haps, argu­ments to be made that com­mu­nism, as prac­ticed in, for exam­ple, the Sovi­et Union, took the form it did pre­cise­ly because it depart­ed from Marx­ist lines. Whether that was bet­ter or worse than the alter­na­tive is a mat­ter no philoso­pher can set­tle.
The clip above comes from the 1952 TV episode A Con­ver­sa­tion with Bertrand Rus­sell. Watch it in full here.

He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: How the Japanese Practice of “Forest Bathing”—Or Just Hanging Out in the Woods—Can Lower Stress Levels and Fight Disease
description: When the U.S. media began report­ing on the phe­nom­e­non of “for­est bathing” as a ther­a­py for men­tal and phys­i­cal health, the online c
body:
When the U.S. media began report­ing on the phe­nom­e­non of “for­est bathing” as a ther­a­py for men­tal and phys­i­cal health, the online commentariat—as it will—mocked the con­cept relent­less­ly as yet anoth­er pre­ten­tious, bour­geois repack­ag­ing of some­thing thor­ough­ly mun­dane. Didn’t we just used to call it “going out­side”?
Well, yes, if all “for­est bathing” means is “going out­side,” then it does sound like a grandiose and unnec­es­sary phrase. The term, how­ev­er, is not an Amer­i­can mar­ket­ing inven­tion but a trans­la­tion of the Japan­ese shin­rin-yoku. “Coined by the Japan­ese Min­istry of Agri­cul­ture, Forestry and Fish­eries in 1982,” writes Meeri Kim at The Wash­ing­ton Post, “the word lit­er­al­ly trans­lates to ‘tak­ing in the for­est atmos­phere’ or ‘for­est bathing’ and refers to the process of soak­ing up the sights, smells and sounds of a nat­ur­al set­ting to pro­mote phys­i­o­log­i­cal and psy­cho­log­i­cal health.”
So what? We already have the exam­ples of thou­sands of years of Bud­dhist monks (and Thich Nhat Hanh), of Hen­ry David Thore­au, and the saints of the Sier­ra Club. But the old­est and most use­ful ideas and prac­tices can get care­less­ly dis­card­ed in the fran­tic pur­suit of inno­va­tion at all costs. The push­ing of hi-tech out­door gear, wear­able activ­i­ty track­ers, and health apps that ask us to log every move­ment can make going out­side feel like a daunt­ing, expen­sive chore or a com­pet­i­tive event.
For­est bathing involves none of those things. “Just be with the trees,” as Ephrat Livni describes the prac­tice, “no hik­ing, no count­ing steps on a Fit­bit. You can sit or mean­der, but the point is to relax rather than accom­plish any­thing.” You don’t have to hug the trees if you don’t want to, but at least sit under one for a spell. Even if you don’t attain enlight­en­ment, you very well may reduce stress and boost immune func­tion, accord­ing to sev­er­al Japan­ese stud­ies con­duct­ed between 2004 and 2012.
The Japan­ese gov­ern­ment spent around four mil­lion dol­lars on stud­ies con­duct­ed with hun­dreds of peo­ple “bathing” on 48 des­ig­nat­ed ther­a­py trails. In his work, Qing Li, asso­ciate pro­fes­sor at Nip­pon Med­ical School in Tokyo, found “sig­nif­i­cant increas­es in NK [nat­ur­al killer] cell activ­i­ty in the week after a for­est vis­it… pos­i­tive effects last­ed a month fol­low­ing each week­end in the woods.” Nat­ur­al killer cells fight virus­es and can­cers, and are appar­ent­ly stim­u­lat­ed by the oils that trees them­selves secrete to ward off germs and pests. See the pro­fes­sor explain in the video above (he trans­lates shin­rin-yoku as tak­ing a “for­est show­er,” and also claims to have bot­tled some of the effects).
Addi­tion­al­ly, exper­i­ments con­duct­ed by Japan’s Chi­ba Uni­ver­si­ty found that for­est bathing low­ered heart rate and blood pres­sure and brought down lev­els of cor­ti­sol, the stress hor­mone that can wreak hav­oc on every sys­tem when large amounts cir­cu­late through the body. Then there are the less tan­gi­ble psy­cho­log­i­cal ben­e­fits of tak­ing in the trees. Sub­jects in one study “showed sig­nif­i­cant­ly reduced hos­til­i­ty and depres­sion scores” after a walk in the woods. These find­ings under­score that spend­ing time in the for­est is a med­ical inter­ven­tion as well as an aes­thet­ic and spir­i­tu­al one, some­thing sci­en­tists have long observed but haven’t been able to quan­ti­fy.
In their review of a book called Your Brain on Nature, Moth­er Earth News quotes Franklin Hough, first chief of the U.S. Divi­sion of Forestry, who remarked in a 19th cen­tu­ry med­ical jour­nal that forests have “a cheer­ful and tran­quil­iz­ing influ­ence which they exert upon the mind, more espe­cial­ly when worn down by men­tal labor.” Hough’s hypoth­e­sis has been con­firmed, and despite what might sound to Eng­lish speak­ers like a slight­ly ridicu­lous name, for­est bathing is seri­ous ther­a­py, espe­cial­ly for the ever-increas­ing num­ber of urban­ites and those who spend their days in strip malls, office com­plex­es, and oth­er over­built envi­ron­ments.
What is a guid­ed for­est bathing expe­ri­ence like? You can lis­ten to NPR’s Ali­son Aubrey describe one above. She quotes Amos Clif­ford, founder of the Asso­ci­a­tion of Nature & For­est Ther­a­py, the cer­ti­fy­ing orga­ni­za­tion, as say­ing that a guide “helps you be here, not there,” sort of like a med­i­ta­tion instruc­tor. Clif­ford has been push­ing health care providers to “incor­po­rate for­est ther­a­py as a stress-reduc­tion strat­e­gy” in the U.S., and there’s no ques­tion that more stress reduc­tion tools are sore­ly need­ed.
But, you may won­der, do you have to call it “for­est bathing,” or pay for a cer­ti­fied guide, join a group, and buy some fan­cy out­er­wear to get the ben­e­fits of hang­ing out with trees? I say, con­sid­er the words of John Muir, the inde­fati­ga­ble 19th cen­tu­ry nat­u­ral­ist, “father of the Nation­al Park Sys­tem,” and found­ing saint of the Sier­ra Club: In the eter­nal youth of Nature you may renew your own. Go qui­et­ly, alone; no harm will befall you. The quote may under­es­ti­mate the amount of risk or over­state the ben­e­fits, but you get the idea. Muir was not one to get tan­gled up in seman­tics or over­ly detailed analy­sis. Nonethe­less, his work inspired Amer­i­cans to step in and pre­serve so much of the coun­try’s for­est in the 19th and 20th cen­turies. Maybe the pre­ven­ta­tive med­i­cine of “for­est bathing” can help do the same in the 21st.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: Meet Lloyd Kahn, the Counterculture Publisher Who Is Skateboarding at 91
description:
in Life |   	September 7th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Lloyd Kahn worked as an insur­ance bro­ker before quit­ting in 1965. Then, he took a tur
body:
in Life |   	September 7th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Lloyd Kahn worked as an insur­ance bro­ker before quit­ting in 1965. Then, he took a turn into the DIY build­ing move­ment that emerged with the 1960s coun­ter­cul­ture. Soon enough, he found him­self edit­ing the influ­en­tial Whole Earth Cat­a­log and pub­lish­ing Shel­ter in 1973, a book still con­sid­ered the bible of hand-built homes. Now 91 years old, Lloyd remains active in pub­lish­ing. He also con­tin­ues to run, pad­dle­board, and skate­board, a sport he took up when he turned 65. How many peo­ple can say that?
In the video above, Sier­ra Clark takes you inside Lloy­d’s world, giv­ing you a snap­shot of his uncon­ven­tion­al life. With a great touch, she high­lights the habits and phi­los­o­phy that have allowed him to live and age in a remark­able way. Stay­ing curi­ous and adven­tur­ous, try­ing new things, keep­ing in motion, eat­ing well, mak­ing life and exer­cise fun—they’re all part of the mix for Lloyd. For Kahn, “Stay hun­gry, stay fool­ish” (the say­ing that appeared on the back of the last Whole Earth Cat­a­log) isn’t just a mot­to. It has been a true way of life.
For more videos focus­ing on longevi­ty and health, vis­it Sier­ra Clark’s YouTube chan­nel here.

title: Henry Wessel's Candid California Photos Underscore the Art of Noticing
description: “There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) sa
body:
“There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) said in a “TateShots” short on the occasion of Tate Modern’s display of his Incidents series in 2014. Today, an exhibition of more than 65 prints titled Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books opens at The Grolier Club, a historic society celebrating the world of books and the graphic arts.
Wessel was a New Jersey native who, after borrowing a Leica camera during his studies at Pennsylvania State University, fell headlong into photography. He rose to prominence in the early 1970s for his black-and-white compositions that plumbed the possibilities of landscape and documentary imagery. Following the receipt of a Guggenheim grant, he moved to the Bay Area, where he taught at the now-defunct San Francisco Art Institute from 1973 to 2014 and captured the area’s characteristically glowing light, historic neighborhoods, and individualistic denizens.
“Untitled” (1968), gelatin silver print
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes the artist’s Incidents and Traffic series in their totality, plus works from his Real Estate and Night Walks series. To make the latter, he would walk around neighborhoods with his tripod and take portraits of local homes after dinner or during the early morning hours.
In Traffic, Wessel snapped scenes and other drivers from his car, capturing candid moments as other vehicles passed or as he encountered roadside curiosities. But he quickly learned that there’s an inherent issue with having to stop the car, get out, and try to capture what you initially saw: it looks totally different.
Wessel began to capture what he saw directly from the driver’s seat, working quickly with the hope that the image would more closely translate his experience. In an SFMOMA interview he said, “You know, like they say, luck is impartial. You have just as much bad luck as you have good luck. But you can do things to prepare yourself to receive the good luck. And that’s part of the whole process of photographing.”
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes some of Wessel’s earliest work, such as “Untitled” from 1968, plus the other series that were created throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The show opens today and continues through November 14 in New York.

title: The Artist Residency That Never Was
description:
Feature
                Abstract Mag invited dozens of artists to participate in a summer residency in Georgia. Then its social
body:
Feature
                Abstract Mag invited dozens of artists to participate in a summer residency in Georgia. Then its social media pages went dark. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            "Rocket" (2026) by Syd Sauer, one of many artists who say they were ghosted by Abstract Mag after applying to their advertised residency (image courtesy Syd Sauer)Like hundreds of other visual artists around the world, 25-year-old airbrush painter Syd Sauer Wilson opened their email inbox on Friday, June 5, to what appeared to be the opportunity of a lifetime: an invitation to participate in an artist residency program hosted by Abstract Mag — a popular art-focused social media platform that had over 1 million followers — taking place overseas this summer.The residency promised an all-expenses-paid retreat in the mountainous regions of southern Georgia, where for two weeks in August, 40 visual artists would live in a “historic chateau” and pursue their practices while also exploring the country’s culture and traditions through a series of expeditions and activities. For the emerging artist hungry for any opportunity to create works in a historic environment without having to pay for travel, materials, or accommodations, a residency like this would be a dream come true.This was the case for Wilson, an early-career artist in Los Angeles. They had applied to last year’s residency, hosted in the 18th-century Château De Forbin in Marseille, for a $40 fee after seeing the open call for artists on Abstract Mag’s social media pages. Though Wilson didn’t apply to this year’s residency in Georgia, they received an email in June from a member of the program’s artist selection committee informing them that, after being shortlisted last year, they were personally invited to participate this August.“We look forward to welcoming you to Georgia this summer,” the end of the email obtained by Hyperallergic reads, with a link that directs the artist to submit more information about their availability, travel information, and any materials they will require during the residency.“ I was super, super excited,” Wilson told Hyperallergic. “I dropped down to the ground on my knees, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God.’ Throughout the day, I just kept looking up at the sky and saying, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’ I called my parents, I shared the news with them, I shared the news with my friends.”But the dream began to crumble after Wilson opened social media to find hundreds of artists coming forward online with reports that they had received similar emails also inviting them to Abstract Mag’s Georgia summer residency this year, raising speculation within the art community about the program’s legitimacy.In July, Abstract Mag announced in since-deleted Instagram posts that 40 artists had been accepted. But artists say they were ghosted after the summer residency’s social media pages all went dark.

title: America in the Making
description:
Announcement
                A new exhibition at the Addison Gallery of American Art examines how art throughout U.S. history reflect
body:
Announcement
                A new exhibition at the Addison Gallery of American Art examines how art throughout U.S. history reflects a growing national identity. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Edward Hopper, Manhattan Bridge Loop, 1928. Oil on canvas, 35 x 60 inches. Gift of Stephen C. Clark, Esq., 1932.17
    
        
            Art serves as a mirror of society — a visual record of the historical, political, and social transformations that shape a culture’s values, struggles, and identity. From the colonial period to the present, American art has registered these shifts, revealing how artists respond to and reinterpret the conditions of their time. America in the Making by the Addison Gallery of American Art, explores how the art of the United States has long expressed the ambition of a nation in formation, through early portraits that recorded new social hierarchies and a fledgling national identity, to 19th-century landscape paintings that celebrated nature while advancing the doctrines of Manifest Destiny and American exceptionalism.As the nation modernized, artists tackled the complexities of 20th-century life, turning away from the visible world by mid-century, and embracing abstraction, the subconscious, and a restless new spirit of individualism and dissent. Today, art continues to respond dynamically in real time to a rapidly changing world and to grapple with the urgent concerns of our present moment.With this exhibition, the Addison Gallery of American Art marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. The entire building will be devoted to a chronological installation of works from the Addison Gallery’s permanent collection. The story of American art told through this collection is neither comprehensive nor objective and  can be read as a window into the conditions, values, and assumptions under which it has been assembled and continues to grow. Its strengths and omissions reflect the circumstances of its formation, including individual taste, institutional priorities, and broader social and cultural forces. In this sense, the exhibition also offers a portrait of a collection in formation, one that, like America itself, remains continually “in the making.”Learn more at addison.andover.edu.

Daily Newsletter
                We recommend art novels, catalogs, memoirs, and more, plus an artist reflects on her portable studio.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            "The History of Narrative Art: Heroes, Myths, the Sacred” at the Lucas Museum features a digital reproduction of the Cave of Altamira. (photo Matt Stromberg/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Watch out, Brooklyn Public Library — there are approximately five dozen intriguing art books coming out this season I’d love to get my hands on. But today, my fellow editors and I narrowed our list down to 15 forthcoming titles we think you should read this fall. From a catalog on Kent Monkman’s response to a Vermeer painting to essays by Elizabeth Alexander, find your next art book below.More reads for your Labor Day weekend, including Matt Stromberg’s dispatch from the ill-fated Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and a glimpse into Rujuta Rao’s portable, modular studio.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

	
		
			15 Art Books for Your Fall Reading List
		
	
	
		Christine Sun Kim’s archive of deafness in pop culture, Guadalupe Rosales’s East Los Angeles memoir, Kent Monkman’s pulls back the curtain on a Vermeer painting — it’s choose your own adventure in art books this fall. We’ve got far too many novels, catalogs, essay collections, and photography books coming out over the next three months to pick from, but these 15 caught our eye. Read on for a story within a story, an artist’s take on Moby-Dick from our resident Mellville fan, Associate Editor Lisa Yin Zhang, and much more. Happy reading! —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
